comments.text:
The worst part was that the country was run by the majority population, who only cared about their own island. Sumatra and Borneo were turned into palm oil plantations, Sulawesi was turned over to nickel mining, and Papua became a site for gold mining yet remained the poorest of all Indonesian provinces.

Meanwhile, Java focused on industrialization and major infrastructure like the high-speed rail. The money spent on it could have been used to connect railway networks across Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, and Papua. Why does this matter? Because the project’s debt is being shifted onto the national budget (APBN), so taxpayers across Indonesia, including those who will never ride it, may end up paying for a line that serves only Jakarta and Bandung. Those of us outside Java share that burden, yet the decisions were made by a central government based on Java.

To be clear, I do not hold animosity toward Javanese people, but toward the unquestioning mentality of the majority, who act like ducklings blindly following a mother into a crocodile’s jaws. In 2024, they chose Prabowo Subianto, a former general who was discharged from the military in 1998 over the abduction of pro-democracy activists, which he has denied and for which he was never tried. His running mate, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, has faced disputes over his educational qualifications. While clearly there exist other candidate with clear background who had Doctoral degree.

I am also very glad that many young Indonesians have finally woken up and begun to protest against the central government, though they are not yet the majority.

It’s strange to think about (I am Dutch).
Indonesia’s total nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is estimated to reach between $1.48 and $1.54 trillion by 2026, whereas the historical peak value of the Dutch East India Company (VOC)—adjusted for the current value of the dollar—is estimated at $7.90 trillion. That is more than the largest company on Earth today (Nvidia, at $5 trillion).

At its absolute financial zenith, the VOC was therefore more than five times as valuable as the entire annual economic output of present-day Indonesia.
For the sake of completeness, I must add that the Dutch behaved like absolute beasts in Indonesia.
